record.original_question: Is the oscillatory sequence [n sin n] good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of powers?

evidence.quote: Problem 28. Show that the sequence ([n sin n]) is good for multiple recurrence and convergence of powers.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denote the integer part of a real number $x$, and consider the integer-valued sequence $a(n) = \lfloor n \sin n\rfloor$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

A sequence $(a(n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ is called good for multiple recurrence of powers if for every invertible measure-preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$, every integer $k\geq 1$, and every $A\in\mathcal{B}$ with $\mu(A)>0$, there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
$$\mu\bigl(A\cap T^{a(n)}A\cap T^{2a(n)}A\cap\cdots\cap T^{k\,a(n)}A\bigr) > 0.$$

It is called good for multiple convergence of powers if for every invertible measure-preserving system $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu,T)$, every integer $k\geq 1$, and all $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in L^\infty(\mu)$, the averages
$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} f_1(T^{a(n)}x)\,f_2(T^{2a(n)}x)\cdots f_k(T^{k\,a(n)}x)$$
converge in $L^2(\mu)$ as $N\to\infty$.

Prove or disprove: the sequence $(\lfloor n\sin n\rfloor)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is good for multiple recurrence of powers and good for multiple convergence of powers.
artifact.status_search_result: Searches for results on whether $\lfloor n\sin n\rfloor$ is good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of powers did not turn up any resolution. Recent work by Bergelson, Moreira, Richter and others on single and multiple recurrence along non-polynomial sequences treats classes such as $\lfloor n^a\rfloor$ and slowly varying functions but does not cover $\lfloor n\sin n\rfloor$, which is non-monotone and not equidistributed in a standard way. No paper claiming a proof or disproof was located, so the problem appears to remain open.
